l.t: Your goal is to build your own data centre: a building full of computers, the kind that trains AI models. You will build every layer yourself, starting at sand.
Every computer in that building runs on chips, and one AI chip, such as NVIDIA's H100, holds about 80 billion tiny switches. This act builds one of those switch
This is a silicon crystal, refined from sand and zoomed in. Every atom holds four bonds, one to each neighbour.
Each bond is a pair of electrons, one contributed by each atom. Both electrons stay locked in the bond.
Tap this atom. Watch what its bond electrons do.
The electrons wobbled and settled back. Every electron is locked in a bond, so nothing can carry a current. Your goal is to make this crystal conduct.
To do that, you dope the crystal: you swap a few silicon atoms for a different element. Pick one:
Phosphorus brings five outer electrons, but a silicon site has only four bonds. Click any three dashed atoms to swap them for phosphorus, and watch where the fi
The fifth electron has no bond to sit in, so it is free to move. It is called a free electron.
Three phosphorus atoms, three free electrons. Silicon carrying spare electrons is called N-type. The N is for negative.
A battery pushes electrons out of its − terminal and pulls them back in at +. The wires reach both faces of the crystal, so any current has to pass through the
Before you doped it, this circuit did nothing. Send current and watch the lamp.
It conducts. The lamp is lit by the free electrons you put in the crystal, drifting across it toward +.Silicon did not change. You gave it carriers. That is wha
Pure silicon barely conducts, and a few atoms of the right element make it conduct. A material like this is called a semiconductor. This is what people mean whe
The blue dots are electrons. They are what actually moves, out of the battery's − terminal and round to +.
People drew current flowing from + to − before electrons were discovered, and real schematics still do. These arrows show that direction, called conventional cu
You will need both kinds of silicon later in this act, so now you will make the other kind, on a fresh crystal.
Here is a fresh crystal. Boron brings three outer electrons, but a silicon site has four bonds to fill. Click any three dashed atoms to swap them for boron, and
The fourth bond is one electron short. This gap, drawn as a red ring, is called a hole.
When an electron from a neighbouring bond hops into the hole, the bond it came from becomes the new hole. So the hole itself appears to move.
Three boron atoms, three holes. Silicon carrying holes is called P-type. A hole moves the way a positive charge would.i
Same test as before. Send current.
It conducts. Inside the crystal the holes drift, with electrons hopping from seat to seat. In the metal wires, ordinary electrons carry the current.Silicon did

In step 1 you doped silicon two ways. Here is one block of each. Your goal is to press them together and find the voltage that pushes a current across the join.
The N block has free electrons. The P block has holes, drawn as rings. Press them together: drag the N block onto the dashed outline, or tap the block and then
There is no battery yet. Watch what the carriers (the free electrons and holes) next to the junction do on their own.
The electrons nearest the junction crossed over and filled the nearest holes. No battery pushed them: electrons spread from where there are many to where there
Each electron that crossed left behind a charged atom, locked in the crystal. The region around the junction now has no free carriers. It is called the depletio
The crossing then stopped on its own: the P side is now slightly negative,i and that pushes the next electron back. Here is that push, drawn as a hill. Watch an
A battery now pushes the carriers toward the depletion layer, and the lamp shows whether current gets through. Your goal is to raise the voltage until current f
The hill is 0.7 V tall.i Below that voltage the electron slid back every time; above it, current flows.
Inside, the battery pushes electrons into the N side and pulls electrons out of the P side, leaving holes. These cancel the charged atoms at the layer's edges,
At 0.7 V the layer is too thin to hold them back. Electrons cross and fill holes on the P side, giving off a little heat, while the battery sends more. That ste
If you turn the battery around, the carriers (electrons and holes) get pulled away from the depletion layer instead of being pushed toward it.
Your goal is to turn the voltage all the way up and confirm that nothing flows. Watch the depletion layer and the hill as you go.
The depletion layer got wider and the hill got taller. In this direction, no voltage gets an electron across.
You have built a diode: a one-way street for current.A voltage raises or lowers the barrier. That control is the basis of every switch in a chip. Copper cannot
IN THE LABHere is the diode you built, sold as a part: the 1N4001. The grey band marks the N side, called the cathode. The P side is the anode. Like yours, it c
IN THE LABAn LED is a diode too, made from other materials, such as gallium nitride. When an electron crosses its junction and fills a hole, it gives off light.
Here is last step's diode. It opens only when the current through it pushes hard enough. A switch needs a separate wire that turns a large current on and off.
If you put two of these junctions back to back, you get a switch you can control. That takes three blocks: N, then a thin P, then N.
Drag each block into a slot, or tap a block and then a slot. The small emitter goes on the left, the thin base in the middle and the wide collector on the right
The emitter sends out the electrons. It is small because its only job is to push electrons into the block next to it.
The base is the thin P block in the middle. Every electron the emitter sends out has to cross it.
The collector collects the electrons that make it across. It is wide because it carries the whole current, and a large current produces heat.
Each junction builds its own depletion layer, just like the single junction did. Because there are two junctions, there are two barriers, facing opposite ways.
Now we connect a battery across the device, from collector to emitter. Because one of the two barriers always faces the wrong way, the LED stays dark.
You already know how to lower a barrier: push about 0.7 V across it. This second battery does that to the left barrier only, so electrons start crossing from th
Those electrons are now in the base, and the base wire is a way out. Where do they go?
A hundred electrons leave the emitter, one after another. This tally counts where each one ends up.
↳ A hundred electrons leave the emitter, one after another. This tally counts where each one ends up.
You were right. 99 of the 100 reached the collector. The base is so thin that an electron is barely inside it before the collector pulls it across.
Now a dial sets how much current you push into the base. The two readouts show that current and the current running through the device from collector to emitter
Your goal is to switch the large current using the small one. First, turn the dial to zero and switch the LED fully off.
With no base current, nothing gets through the device. Now turn the dial up to 10 µA and take the LED to full brightness.
You put 10 µA in, and 1,000 µA came out. The small base current keeps the first barrier lowered, so a hundred times more current passes.Flick the dial and it is
N, a thin P, then N: this is an NPN transistor, a switch with no moving parts. This is what people mean when they talk about a chip's transistor count: a count
IN THE LABHere is the NPN transistor you just built, sold as a part: a BC547. Before chips, whole computers were built from thousands of separate transistors li
Here is last step's transistor, switched on. To stay on, it needs about 10 µA flowing into its base the whole time, and a chip holds billions of transistors.
So instead, we will control the transistor with a voltage, so that nothing has to keep flowing. Your goal is to build this new transistor one layer at a time, t
Start with a block of P-type silicon, full of holes. Drag an N patch onto each end, so that each end is packed with spare electrons.
Between the two patches is a strip of P silicon with no spare electrons, so nothing can cross this gap. Our whole job is to close this gap on demand.
Two tiles are left: a thin sheet of glass and a metal pad. One of them goes straight onto the silicon, over the gap. Drag it in.
Now place the metal pad on top of the glass. It sits directly over the gap and never touches the silicon. This pad is called the gate.
Electrons enter at the source and leave at the drain. Wire a battery across them, plus at the drain and minus at the source, and try to push a current through.
The current is blocked. The hatched bands are depletion layers, the same barriers you built in step 2. There are two junctions, and one of them always faces the
Metal, glass and silicon form a capacitor (two conducting plates with an insulator between them). Charging the top plate costs no steady current, because the gl
If you put a small positive voltage on the gate, the positive plate pushes the holes underneath it downward, away from the glass.
If you keep going, the same field pulls electrons up out of the silicon and holds them against the underside of the glass.
With a little more voltage, that sheet of electrons reaches both N regions, and the source and drain become one unbroken path.
The lamp is lit. Current runs from drain to source through a sheet of electrons that only exists while the gate voltage is held high.Nothing went into the gate
The slider is yours now. If you push the gate voltage higher, the sheet gets denser and more current flows. Your goal is to switch it fully on, above 2.6 V.
Now bring it back down. The sheet breaks the moment the gate voltage drops below 1.2 V. Your goal is to switch it fully off, below 0.3 V.
Your transistor from last step and this new transistor can both stay on all day. Which one is cheaper to hold on?
You were right. Holding a voltage on the gate costs no ongoing current, because the glass never lets charge through. The NPN transistor has to keep consuming ba
The three layers name the device: metal, oxide (the glass),i semiconductor. It is called a MOSFET, and yours is an NMOS, because a high gate voltage fills its c

Here is that NMOS, placed between two rails. The top rail carries the supply voltage, and the bottom rail is ground, at 0 V. A high gate joins the two rails thr

A wire from the middle of the column ends at OUT. The circle lights when the output is high, marked 1, and goes dark when it is low, marked 0. It only stands in

It is wired. The input connects to both gates at once. It is high right now, so the bottom transistor conducts and the top one is off. Exactly one of them is ev
Set the input to 0 and watch the output lamp.
Now set the input to 1.
Input 0 gave output 1. Input 1 gave output 0. The output is always the opposite of the input, so this pair is called an inverter (it inverts the input).
This is what people mean when they say a computer works in 0s and 1s. Each 1 or 0 is a wire held high or low, like your input and your output. Your inverter set
Now watch the meter instead of the lamp. Flip the input twice more.
The needle only twitched on each flip. Between flips, one of the two transistors is always off, so there is no path from power to ground.The only current is the
This pair is one N-type transistor and one P-type transistor, wired against each other. It is called complementary MOS, or CMOS.
This is where a chip's heat comes from. Each twitch of the needle is a little energy that ends up as heat in the pair. Billions of pairs flipping make most of a

Four transistors give one answer: the output is 0 only when both inputs are 1. The name for a gate that does this is NAND, short for not both.
If you tie both inputs to one wire, they are always equal. Feed that wire a 1 and the output is 0. The NAND now works as an inverter, also called a NOT gate.
If you put a NAND in front of that NOT gate, the 0 flips back to 1. The pair now outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1, and that is an AND gate.
NOT and AND both came out of the same NAND gate, wired two different ways.That is what makes NAND a universal gate: any logic you can describe can be built from

End of step → Add two numbers ▸
You already know this one: 5 + 3 = 8. Here you build the circuit that gets there, and check it against the answer you started with.
Here are four lamps. Each holds one bit: a 0 when dark, a 1 when lit. Each also has a weight, 8, 4, 2, 1, called place value. Add the weights of the lit lamps t
This row reads 8 + 4 + 1 = 13. Your goal is to make it read 9.
One lamp can only show 0 or 1. 1 + 1 is 2, which does not fit in a single lamp, so the answer spills into the lamp on its left. That spill is called the carry.
Here is the same sum on paper, in binary (numbers written with only the digits 0 and 1). 5 is 101i and 3 is 011. Work it one column at a time, starting at the r
Ones column: 1 + 1 = 2. Two does not fit here, so write 0 in this column and pass 1 to the column on the left.
In the twos column, 0 + 1 plus the carried 1 makes 2. In the fours column, 1 + 0 plus the carried 1 makes 2 again. Each time, write 0 and pass 1 left.
Nothing left to add in the eights column, but a carry is still coming in from the right. It lands here as a 1.
The sum row reads 1000. Add the weights of the lit columns: 8. The paper method lands on the answer you already had.
Every column did the same job: add two digits and the carry in, write one digit, and pass any carry left. You will build that job once as a circuit, then copy i
The circuit that does one column is a full adder, shown here as five empty boxes. It takes three inputs: the digits A and B, and the carry in from the right. It
The sum digit is 1 when the two digits differ. The gate that asks "do these differ?" is XOR (exclusive or). There are two here, because the carry in has to be c
The carry asks a different question: were both digits 1? AND answers that, once for A and B, and once for the carry in. Either one is enough, so OR (output 1 if
Your goal is to place the five gates. The caption under each empty box says which question that box answers.
Your five gates are live now. Your goal is to make SUM read 0 while CARRY OUT reads 1.
SUM reads 0 and CARRY OUT reads 1. The column kept 0 and handed the carry to the column on its left, the same move you made on paper.
The five gates now sit inside one box, the full adder. Here it is stamped four times, once per column, in place value order: eights, fours, twos, ones.
Each full adder's carry out feeds the carry in of the one on its left. Every carry waits for the column on its right, so the answer settles from right to left.
The answer row has five lamps, because four columns only hold up to 15. Your goal is to set A to 5 and B to 3, using the bit buttons under the stage.
The answer is 8. The carry moved right to left, one column at a time, the same way you did it on paper.Every addition a computer does is built from this same co

End of step → Keep an answer after you let go ▸
This is your ripple adder from step 2. Press and hold the button below. While you hold it, the rows read 5 and 3 and the sum reads 8. Then let go.
When the inputs went to 0, the sum went with them. The adder only reports what is on its wires right now.
Here are two NAND gates. To keep an answer after its inputs go, a circuit feeds its outputs back in. Wiring each gate's output into the other gate's input is ca
Your goal is to close the loop. Click the pin (the end point of a wire) the stage marks, then the one it marks next. You will draw two wires in all.
Two more wires come in from the left: S into gate 1, and R into gate 2. This lamp shows gate 1's output, and that output is the bit you are storing.i
Two NANDs wired like this are an SR latch, which holds one bit. S sets it to 1 and R resets it to 0. Both wires sit at 1, and each button pulls its wire to 0 wh
A NAND's output is 1 whenever any input is 0. So holding S forces gate 1's output to 1. Holding R forces gate 2's output to 1, and that drives gate 1's output t
Store a 1. Hold S, then take your finger off.
Store a 0. Hold R, then let go. MEMORY goes dark and stays dark.
In Act 1 you built a switch, then a CMOS pair that holds its output high or low while drawing almost no current. These two NAND gates are built the same way.
The SR latch remembers because each gate's output keeps the other gate's input where it was, even after you let go.This is what people mean when they say a comp
This loop is what SRAM is. The cache in a processor, its small fast memory, is millions of these loops, each built with 6 transistors instead of your 8.i
One SR latch holds one bit. Four side by side are a register: a circuit that holds a whole number. These four are holding 11.
Your register holds 4 bits. Eight bits together are a byte, which holds a number from 0 to 255. Memory is counted in bytes, so 16 GB is about 16 billion bytes.

IN THE LABThe charge leaks away, so the chip rewrites every bit at least once every 64 ms. The HBM in Act 4 is DRAM too.
End of step → Make them run on their own ▸
Three parts are on the bench, one from each step so far: the NAND gate, the ripple adder, and the register, which holds a four-bit number until something tells
The wires are already in place. One slot needs the part that holds a number, and the other needs the part that adds to it. Your goal is to fill both slots. One
The top wire carries the number from the register into the adder, and the lower wire brings the answer back, in a closed loop. A third wire brings up the addend
The clock is a signal that pulses at a steady rate, and one cycle is one beat. The register only takes a new value on a beat.i
The clock is a separate circuit, like a metronome: it beats at a fixed rate and does not wait for the adder. If a beat arrives before the sum is finished, the r
A clock's speed is counted in hertz (Hz), one beat per second. When a laptop chip is sold as 4.7 GHz (gigahertz), its clock beats 4.7 billion times a second. Fo
Each cycle has three phases: fetch the number out of the register, compute the sum, and store it back. Set an addend on the switches, then run three cycles.
Four bits can only count up to 15. The register is now set to 14, with 5 on the addend.
14 plus 5 is 19. Nineteen needs a sixteens bit, and four bits have none, so the register dropped the sixteens bit and kept the 3. It wrapped round, like an odom
Your register holds 4 bits, so this is a 4-bit machine. A 64-bit chip has 64-bit registers and a 64-column adder, so it counts past 18 quintillion before it wra
Make the register read exactly 12
So far you pressed a button for every beat. The register is back at 0, with 1 on the addend. Switch the clock to RUN, and it beats by itself, about once a secon
Your loop just ran by itself: fetch, compute, store, and repeat. If it runs a few billion times a second, you have a CPU (central processing unit, the chip that
One copy of this loop, with the parts that steer it,i is called a core. A laptop chip with 8 cores runs 8 of these loops side by side.
Your machine has a few hundred transistors, placed by hand. A phone chip has 19 billion. Nobody places those by hand: they are printed.
Here is everything you built in this act, from one NAND gate to a machine that runs by itself.

In Act 2 you built a small processor as a drawing. To make it real, every transistor has to sit on silicon that is one unbroken crystal, the ordered grid of ato
This is the melt: refined sand, 99.9999999% silicon,i held liquid at 1,414 °C. Purity is not enough on its own, because every atom still has to land in the righ
The rod holds a seed crystal, a small bar of silicon whose atoms already sit in perfect order. Touch it to the melt and pull it back up: silicon freezes onto it
The panel magnifies the growth face, where the crystal meets the melt. Each circle is one silicon atom, and the ones below the dashed line are still liquid. An
That layer is about 0.14 nm thick. A finished ingot (the whole grown crystal) is 1.6 m of such layers, every atom sitting where the row below it says.
Pull speed decides how well each layer lands. Run a short test pull at all three speeds and watch the growth face. Your goal is a full ingot with no breaks (mis
At 1.5 mm/min the row closes before every atom has arrived. Each gap left behind is a permanent break in the lattice.
At 0.2 mm/min, extra silicon atoms have time to squeeze between the rows and clump.i
One speed filled every site (every place in the lattice where an atom belongs). Pick that speed for the full 1.6 m pull.
Here is one crystal, 300 mm across, 1.6 m long and about 265 kg. Its lattice runs unbroken from the seed to the bottom. This way of growing a crystal is called

One pull gives more than a thousand wafers. Each one will carry billions of the transistors you built by hand in Act 1.A single wafer holds more transistors tha

You cannot place billions of transistors by hand, and a fab does not place them either. It prints them onto a wafer like this one, with light, one layer at a ti
First the wafer is coated with photoresist (resist for short), a thin film whose chemistry changes wherever light lands on it. This is the coat step.
Above it sits the mask. A mask works like a stencil: it is a clear plate with this layer's pattern drawn on it in metal. Light passes through the gaps and is st
Here is a mask from above: a square plate of quartz glass about 15 cm across. The machine shrinks its pattern four times as it prints it onto one patch of the w
NVIDIA and Apple own no fab. They send their designs, the patterns for every mask, to a foundry: a company whose fabs print other companies' chips. This is what
Zoom into one tiny spot of that pattern, and its shapes are the parts of transistors like the NMOS you built in Act 1: a source and a drain, with a gatei sittin
A gate's length is how far it stretches from the source side to the drain side, the distance electrons cross under it. The mask sets this length for every gate
The machine flashes light down at the mask. Whatever gets through carries the pattern to the resist below.
This is a positive resist: light breaks it down. Every patch the light reached is now soluble, which means it will dissolve in the developer liquid used next. T
Next comes develop: the wafer is rinsed in an alkaline (basic) liquid. The soluble patches dissolve away and the solid resist stays, which leaves openings in ex
Developing removed only resist, so the silicon under each opening has not changed yet. Next comes etch: a gas or liquid eats away the silicon through each openi
Then dope: phosphorus atoms, a doping element from Act 1, are fired at the wafer. They reach the silicon only through the openings, so only the pattern turns N-
Last, the leftover resist is stripped off, which leaves the silicon with this layer's pattern cut and doped into it.
That is one finished layer. It has no wires yet. The metal wires that join transistors into gates are printed later, in layers stacked on top, using this same l
Here is a slice through a finished chip, seen from the side. The transistors are the thin band at the bottom. Above them are 15 layers of copper wires, kept apa
You have now run all five steps. They only work in one order. Your goal is to put them back in that order: drag each tile into a slot, or tap a tile and then a
Coat, expose, develop, etch, dope: this loop is called photolithography (printing a pattern with light). The resist is then stripped off and the loop runs again
Now look down from above at a later layer, on top of the transistors. The five rings are vias: holes left open so that the metal of the wiring layer printed abo
Here are the same layers, seen from the side. Glass is laid over the transistors in the silicon. Then a printing pass etches a via down through it above each so
Metal fills the vias, and another printing pass etches it into wires that touch the transistors. Then glass, vias and wires repeat, layer on layer. A whole chip
Layer two's mask is out of place. On a real wafer, an error of a couple of nanometres means the metal misses the via. Your goal is to bring both offsets, shown
Both offsets are zero, so the metal that goes in next will touch. The newest machines print this way with extreme ultraviolet light, 13.5 nanometres long. Only
Shorter light prints smaller shapes, so more transistors fit in the same area. Each new generation is called a process node, with a name such as 5 nm or 3 nm. T
Each node has fitted roughly twice as many transistors in the same area, about every two years since the 1970s. This is Moore's law. When you read that it is sl
